listenings.text: When somebody attacks your position in public, your instinct is to defend it immediately. Resist that for five seconds. The most powerful move in a hostile exchange is to restate the other person's argument so fairly that they say, yes, exactly. It does three things. It shows the room you were listening. It forces the other person to agree with you about what the disagreement actually is. And it gives you time to think. Only then should you concede what is true, and there is almost always something true. After that, push back on the one point that matters, and turn it into a hypothesis the room can discuss. People can argue with a hypothesis for an hour without anybody losing face. They cannot do that with an accusation.

Thank you, David, and I am going to stop you there, because I want to make sure the room has your main point before we lose it. If I understand you correctly, what you are saying is that the auction calendar, not the tariff, is what keeps investors away. Is that fair? Good. Now, that is a claim the fund side will want to test, so let me bring in Maria. Maria, you have been shaking your head for two minutes. Should the calendar be fixed by law, as David suggests, would your fund bid in the first round, or would you still wait? And a caveat for everyone: we have eleven minutes left, so I will ask you to keep your answers under ninety seconds.
